title: Logo File Formats Explained: Vector, PNG, SVG, PDF and More
h1: Logo file formats explained: what to ask your designer for
description: Which logo files you need and why: vector vs raster, AI, EPS, SVG, PDF, PNG and JPG, color versions, and a simple checklist to use before you accept a logo.
intro: A logo is only as useful as the files you receive. Many buyers approve a design they love, then discover months later that they only have a small image that looks blurry on a banner or cannot be printed on a shirt. Understanding a few file types, and asking for the right ones before the order ends, saves time and money later. This article explains the formats in plain language and gives you a checklist to use when your logo is delivered.

faq.q: What is the most important logo file?
faq.a: A vector master file, usually AI, EPS, SVG or PDF. All other versions can be created from it.

faq.q: Can I turn a PNG logo into a vector?
faq.a: A designer can redraw it as a vector. This is called vector tracing and is a common service.

faq.q: Which format should I use on my website?
faq.a: SVG for sharp results at any size, or PNG with a transparent background.

faq.q: What format does a printer need?
faq.a: Usually a vector PDF or EPS, and sometimes the exact color codes for print.

faq.q: Do I need the fonts too?
faq.a: If your logo uses text, ask for the font names and licenses, or for the text converted to outlines.
